set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: How does the Hounsfield table refine the five basic radiographic densities?
opts: It separates fat from air, which a conventional radiograph cannot tell apart
Fat and air are already distinguishable on a plain film.
It merges bone and soft tissue, which a conventional radiograph shows separately
The table separates tissues rather than merging them.
It separates water from soft tissue, which a conventional radiograph cannot tell apart
Correct — the deck's asterisk on “Five*” marks exactly that exception.
It separates calcium from metal, which a conventional radiograph cannot tell apart
Calcium and metal are already distinct among the five basic densities.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: Ordered from the most negative Hounsfield number to the most positive, what is the sequence of tissues?
opts: Fat, air, water, bone, soft tissue, metal
Air is more negative than fat, and bone is denser than soft tissue.
Air, fat, water, soft tissue, bone, metal
Correct — and it runs blackest to whitest in exactly that order.
Air, water, fat, soft tissue, bone, metal
Fat is negative and water is zero, so fat comes first.
Metal, bone, soft tissue, water, fat, air
This is the correct sequence reversed.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Which substance is assigned a Hounsfield number of zero by convention?
opts: Air
Air sits at the low, negative end of the scale.
Bone
Bone sits at the high, positive end of the scale.
Fat
Fat sits below water on the scale but is not the zero reference.
Water
Correct — other tissues take a range of Hounsfield numbers according to their density.

set1.io: h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What does the deck say about shellfish allergy and iodinated contrast?
opts: There is cross-reactivity only with the iso-osmolal agents such as iodixanol
The deck draws no agent-specific exception of this kind.
There should be no cross-reactivity between shellfish and iodinated radiocontrast
Correct — the cross-reactivity idea is explicitly rejected.
There is well-established cross-reactivity, so the two allergies must be treated as one
This is the belief the deck corrects rather than the position it takes.
There is partial cross-reactivity, so contrast may be given at a reduced concentration
No such graded approach is described; the cross-reactivity itself is denied.

set1.io: a — Identify the fundamental properties of medical imaging
set1.q: Who discovered x-rays, and what recognition followed?
opts: Wilhelm Roentgen, in Germany in 1895, awarded the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901
Correct — the technique is still called roentgenography after him.
Godfrey Hounsfield, in Britain in 1972, awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1979
He developed the first computed tomography scanner, with Allan Cormack.
Allan Cormack, in South Africa in 1963, awarded the first Nobel Prize for Physics
He shared the 1979 Medicine prize for computed tomography.
Marie Curie, in France in 1898, awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1903
Her work was on radioactivity rather than the discovery of x-rays.

set1.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: Which phrase did Professor Reynolds call out as a buzzword, and what does it mean?
opts: Coral-red fluorescence — erythrasma
That is a dermatology finding from a different course.
Increased attenuation — a metallic foreign body
Attenuation is computed tomography vocabulary rather than the buzzword named.
Free air under the diaphragm — perforated bowel
Correct — unless there has been recent laparoscopic surgery and the insufflated gas is not yet absorbed.
Air-fluid levels in dilated loops — small bowel obstruction
Obstruction is a named indication for the series, but it is not the phrase she flagged.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: Which term describes tissue that appears white because it absorbs more of the beam?
opts: Radiopaque, also called hyperdense or radiodense
Correct — less passage of x-ray photons produces the whiter appearance.
Radiolucent, also called hypodense
That describes darker tissue with greater photon passage.
Isodense, matching the density of the surrounding tissue
That term is not the one for a white appearance.
Attenuated, meaning the beam has been scattered away
Increased attenuation is a computed tomography term for the same idea.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: What is the window in computed tomography?
opts: The interval during which the contrast sits at its peak concentration in the vessel
That is a timing concept rather than the display window.
The slice thickness selected before the scan is acquired
Slice thickness is a separate acquisition parameter.
The range of Hounsfield numbers pre-selected for display, spread over the available grey scale
Correct — for example only those densities between −100 and +300.
The physical aperture of the gantry through which the patient passes
That is the bore rather than the window.

set1.io: h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What must be checked before giving intravenous iodinated contrast, and why?
opts: Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, because the agent is nephrotoxic
Correct — and a litre of normal saline is given to protect the kidneys.
Liver function tests and bilirubin, because the agent is cleared hepatically
The concern named is renal rather than hepatic.
Thyroid function tests, because the iodine load can precipitate thyrotoxicosis
Thyroid effects are real clinically but are not what this deck requires checking.
Complete blood count and platelets, because the agent affects coagulation
Coagulation is not the risk the deck attaches to iodinated contrast.

set1.io: f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: In the deck's table of typical organ radiation doses, which listed study delivers the highest dose?
opts: Barium enema, to the colon
Fifteen, which is high but is not the top of the table.
Adult abdominal computed tomography, to the stomach
Ten, which is half the neonatal figure.
Screening mammography, to the breast
Three, well below the abdominal tomography studies.
Neonatal abdominal computed tomography, to the stomach
Correct — twenty, the largest figure in the table.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Which tracer does positron emission tomography typically use, and why that one?
opts: Gadolinium, a paramagnetic metal, because tumours disrupt the local magnetic environment
Gadolinium is the magnetic resonance contrast agent and emits no radiation.
Fluorodeoxyglucose-18, a radioactive glucose, because tumours have a higher metabolic rate
Correct — the scan asks which tissues are consuming more glucose.
Technetium-99, a metastable isotope, because tumours retain it far longer than normal tissue
Technetium-99 is the usual single photon emission tomography agent, tracking blood flow.
Iodixanol, an iso-osmolal agent, because tumours take up iodine more avidly than muscle
Iodixanol is an intravascular iodinated contrast for angiography, not a nuclear tracer.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What does the colour Doppler setting add to a standard ultrasound image?
opts: Depth of penetration and resolution, on an image otherwise limited to superficial planes
Colour Doppler does not extend depth; poor deep visualisation remains a limitation.
Density in Hounsfield units and windowing, on an image otherwise showing five densities
Hounsfield units and windowing belong to computed tomography, not to ultrasound.
Metabolic uptake and intensity, on an image otherwise showing only anatomical structure
Uptake displayed by intensity is how the positron emission studies are read.
Direction of flow and velocity, on an image otherwise made of white, grey and black
Correct — colour is the flow overlay, and blood is what it is used for.

set1.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What are the midsagittal and parasagittal planes?
opts: Midsagittal runs through the umbilicus; parasagittal sections lie above and below it
Both sagittal planes are vertical and separate right from left, not upper from lower.
Midsagittal runs across the shoulders; parasagittal sections lie anterior and posterior
That division is coronal rather than sagittal.
Midsagittal runs at the level of the heart; parasagittal sections are angled off the axis
The distinction is position relative to the midline, not level or angle.
Midsagittal runs in the body's midline; parasagittal sections lie to either side of it
Correct — the midsagittal plane is also called the median plane.

set1.io: f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: Which disadvantages are named for conventional radiography?
opts: Operator dependence and an inability to penetrate bone or large gas-filled structures
Those are the disadvantages of ultrasound.
Long scan times and safety problems with magnetic implanted devices
Those are the disadvantages of magnetic resonance imaging.
Very high radiation dose and an inability to be made portable at all
The dose is described as relatively low and the machines can be portable.
A limited range of densities and reliance on ionizing radiation, though at relatively low dose
Correct — the dose is low compared with other radiographic modalities.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What does single photon emission computed tomography measure, and what does it show?
opts: Attenuated x-rays on a rotating detector ring, giving cross-sectional images by density
Attenuation by density is computed tomography, which measures the beam it transmits.
Single photons on rotating gamma cameras, giving three-dimensional images of where blood flows
Correct — the deck's stated indication is seeing where blood flows to.
Paired positrons on a stationary gamma camera, giving two-dimensional images of glucose uptake
Positrons and glucose uptake are positron emission tomography, not this study.
Reflected sound on a hand-held transducer, giving real-time images of moving structures
Reflected sound in real time is ultrasonography, which injects no tracer.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Which advantages are named for computed tomography?
opts: It is superior to magnetic resonance imaging for differentiating soft tissues
Magnetic resonance imaging is superior for soft tissue.
It expands the grey scale beyond the five basic densities, reduces overlapping of structures, works with implantable devices, and allows three-dimensional reconstruction
Correct — it is described as the cornerstone of cross-sectional imaging.
It uses no ionizing radiation at all and is described as being the safest of all of the imaging modalities that are currently available anywhere
That describes ultrasound.
It is fully portable, inexpensive, and can be brought to the patient's bedside
It is described as not truly portable.

set1.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What does the deck call the most important thing to remember about ultrasound orientation?
opts: Which frequency is selected: high for superficial structures, low for deeper structures
Transducer frequency is a resolution and penetration trade-off, not orientation.
Where the indicator is: on the right of the screen in cardiac imaging, on the left for everything else
Correct — it is called crucial, because the whole image flips with it.
Where the indicator is: on the left of the screen in cardiac imaging, on the right for everything else
This reverses the convention the deck gives for the heart.
How deep the focus is set: shallow for superficial structures, deep for abdominal structures
Focal depth matters for image quality but is not the orientation rule stated.

set1.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: Why can magnetic resonance imaging show tissues that are surrounded by bone better than computed tomography can?
opts: Bone is windowed out during acquisition, so only the soft tissue range is displayed
Windowing is a computed tomography display technique, not a magnetic resonance one.
Bone absorbs the radio waves, so the surrounding soft tissue returns a relatively brighter signal
Bone does not absorb the radiofrequency signal in the way this describes.
Calcium emits no signal, so the bone does not obscure what sits inside it
Correct — silence from calcium is an advantage rather than a gap.
Calcium emits a strong signal, so the bone can be subtracted from the image afterwards
Calcium is silent on magnetic resonance; there is no strong signal to subtract.

set1.io: h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: Professor Reynolds said renal function must be checked before gadolinium, but for a different reason from iodinated contrast. What is that reason?
opts: Gadolinium is far more nephrotoxic than iodinated contrast, so the threshold for withholding it is lower
She said the opposite: gadolinium is not necessarily nephrotoxic.
Gadolinium is cleared hepatically, so renal function predicts the hepatic reserve
The clearance route in question is renal.
Gadolinium interferes with the creatinine assay, so a baseline is needed for comparison
No assay interference is described.
It is a clearance problem — poor function lets it build up in tissue

Correct — gadolinium is not necessarily nephrotoxic itself, but if the kidney cannot clear it, it accumulates in tissue and that accumulation is toxic. With iodinated contrast the agent itself is nephrotoxic.

set1.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: What method did Professor Reynolds give for choosing a modality when you are not certain of the diagnosis?
opts: Always order both a plain film and a cross-sectional study at the same visit
Ordering in parallel is not what she recommended.
Memorise a protocol for each presenting complaint and follow it exactly
She allowed that this works, but named reasoning from the tissue as the fallback.
Reason from the tissue rather than from a memorised protocol
Correct — bone points to x-ray or computed tomography; soft tissue often starts with ultrasound. Memorised protocols are fine, but reasoning from the tissue is what generalises.
Always begin with the study carrying the least radiation and escalate only if negative
Dose matters in the diagnostic approach, but this is not the method she described.

set1.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: Which enteric pathologies is the abdominal series named as evaluating?
opts: Small bowel obstruction, perforation and volvulus
Correct — the three named examples of enteric pathology.
Appendicitis, diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease
These are not the examples the deck gives for the plain abdominal series.
Cholelithiasis, pancreatitis and hepatic abscess
These hepatobiliary conditions are not named for this study.
Peptic ulceration, gastritis and oesophageal stricture
Luminal mucosal disease is assessed with oral contrast rather than a plain series.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What determines the frequency of the radio waves a magnetic resonance scanner reads?
opts: The chemical environment of the hydrogen atoms, together with their location
Correct — both, which is what lets the computer build a spatial map.
The strength of the magnet in Tesla, together with the duration of the scan
Field strength changes image quality, but it is not what the deck names here.
The density of the tissue in Hounsfield units, together with the chosen window
Hounsfield units and windows belong to computed tomography.
The metabolic rate of the tissue, together with the dose of tracer given
Metabolic rate and tracer dose describe nuclear medicine studies.

set1.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: Which density is described as the most dense naturally occurring material?
opts: Calcium
Correct — it absorbs most x-rays, though metal absorbs essentially all of them.
Metal
Metal is denser but is not naturally occurring in the body.
Fluid
Fluid and soft tissue share a middle density.
Fat
Fat is less dense than soft tissue.

set1.io: g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: Which vascular magnetic resonance studies are performed without contrast?
opts: Coronary angiography and retrograde pyelography
Both of these are performed with injected contrast material.
Arthrography and intrathecal myelography
Both are defined by contrast being injected into a space.
Magnetic resonance angiography and magnetic resonance venography
Correct — both are done without a contrast agent.
Computed tomography angiography and computed tomography venography
The computed tomography vascular studies do require an iodinated injection.

set1.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: In which patients is ultrasound named as often the first study of choice?
opts: Female pelvis and paediatric patients, and it is also used to guide procedures
Correct — no radiation is the reason it leads in both groups.
Adult chest and geriatric patients, and it is also used to screen for fractures
Air in the lung and bone both defeat ultrasound; these are radiographic studies.
Head-injured and intoxicated patients, and it is also used to exclude a bleed
Intracranial haemorrhage is a computed tomography question in the adult skull.
Oncology and post-operative patients, and it is also used to stage known disease
Staging is a computed tomography and positron emission tomography role.

set1.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: What does an abdominal series evaluate, and how is the patient positioned?
opts: The gastrointestinal tract, with the patient standing, to assess air-fluid levels or free air
Correct — upright is what makes free air and air-fluid levels visible.
The genitourinary tract, with the patient supine, to assess stones within the collecting system
Supine and urinary describes the kidney-ureter-bladder film instead.
The gastrointestinal tract, with the patient supine, to assess bowel wall thickness and oedema
The series is shot standing, and wall thickness is not what it is described as assessing.
The retroperitoneum, with the patient in decubitus, to assess the psoas shadows and the flanks
Decubitus positioning is described for pleural effusion, not for this study.

set1.io: h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What is given alongside intravenous iodinated contrast to protect the kidneys?
opts: One dose of intravenous furosemide
Forcing diuresis is not what the deck describes for renal protection here.
One litre of normal saline
Correct — the only volume the deck specifies, and it is renal protection.
One litre of lactated Ringer's
The deck names normal saline specifically rather than a balanced solution.
One gram of acetylcysteine
Acetylcysteine is not mentioned in this lecture.

set1.io: i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set1.q: What practical ordering point does the deck make about imaging several body regions?
opts: Multiple body parts must be imaged on separate days to limit cumulative radiation dose
Magnetic resonance emits no ionizing radiation, and no such rule is stated.
Multiple body parts or sections may mean multiple orders, giving brain, cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine as the example
Correct — one clinical question can require four separate requests.
Multiple body parts should be combined into one single order, so that the patient is scanned once and the radiologist reads the whole study together
The deck makes the opposite point about how these studies are requested.
Multiple body parts require the radiologist to countersign the request before booking
No countersignature requirement is described.

set1.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: How does a computed tomography scanner acquire its data?
opts: A gamma camera mounted on a rotating gantry detects the photons that are emitted from an injected isotope
That describes single photon emission computed tomography.
High-frequency sound waves released from a transducer bounce off tissue and return
That describes ultrasound.
A varying magnetic field aligns hydrogen atoms which then emit radio waves
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.
Powerful x-ray beams pass through the patient via a rotating fan beam, measuring transmission at thousands of data points
Correct — a computer then processes the data through algorithms into diagnostic images.

set1.io: f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: How does the lung dose of a lateral chest radiograph compare with the posterior-anterior view?
opts: It is identical, because both views expose the same volume of lung tissue
The table gives two different values for the two projections.
It is higher, but only in children, because the chest wall is thinner
The table is not stratified by age for the chest views.
It is higher, which is one reason the posterior-anterior view is the preferred projection
Correct — the deck also credits the posterior-anterior view with lower dose to sensitive organs.
It is lower, which is one reason the lateral view is taken first in a standard series
The lateral figure in the table is the larger of the two.

set2.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: What is the decubitus position used to evaluate?
opts: Pleural effusion, because gravity lets the fluid around the lung level out and be seen
Correct — fluid in the pleural space moves when the patient is laid on their side.
Free air under the diaphragm, because gravity lets the air rise to the highest point
Free intraperitoneal air is sought on an upright abdominal series.
Bowel obstruction, because gravity separates the air from the fluid within the loops
Air-fluid levels within bowel are assessed on the abdominal series.
Aortic calcification, because gravity displaces the overlying bowel gas out of the field
The decubitus view is not described for vascular calcification here.

set2.io: i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set2.q: Why does the deck stress giving the radiologist relevant clinical information?
opts: The radiologist selects the modality, so the history determines which scanner is booked
They can guide the choice, but the reason stated here is the quality of the read.
The radiologist repeats the study otherwise, so the history prevents duplicate imaging
Avoiding repeat imaging is described as a benefit of post-processing instead.
The radiologist has not seen the patient, so the history is what guides their read
Correct — the report is only as good as the question it is answering.
The radiologist bills separately, so the indication must be documented for the claim
Billing is not the reason the deck gives for communicating.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What are ultrasonography's stated indications?
opts: Assessment of bony structures, naming the skull, the vertebrae and the long bones
Ultrasound cannot penetrate bone, so these are radiographic or tomographic studies.
Assessment of aerated structures, naming the lungs, the sinuses and the bowel gas pattern
Large gas-filled structures disrupt the signal, which is a stated limitation.
Assessment of metabolic activity, naming tumour staging, brain function and perfusion
Metabolic activity is what the nuclear medicine studies are indicated for.
Assessment of moving structures, naming the heart, the vasculature and obstetrics
Correct — it records in real time, which is what suits it to motion.

set2.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Which patient does Professor Reynolds say will get an anterior-posterior chest film rather than a posterior-anterior one?
opts: A sick inpatient who cannot get out of bed
Correct — they cannot stand against a wall, so they are filmed anterior-posterior in bed. Which is exactly why reading the view label matters in practice.
Any patient in whom cardiomegaly is suspected
The anterior-posterior view magnifies the heart, so it is the worse view for that question.
Any paediatric patient, because of the lower dose
The posterior-anterior view is the one credited with lower dose to sensitive organs.
Any patient having a follow-up rather than a first study
Follow-up status is not what determines the projection.

set2.io: h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: Which safety issues are named for magnetic resonance imaging?
opts: Nephrotoxicity and anaphylaxis to iodine, and it is still not recommended in renal impairment
Iodinated contrast belongs to computed tomography; this study uses gadolinium.
Operator dependence and poor penetration of bone, and it is still not recommended in obesity
Those are ultrasound limitations rather than magnetic resonance safety issues.
Magnetic implanted devices and ferromagnetic projectiles, and it is still not recommended in pregnancy or infants
Correct — no radiation is emitted, but the magnet itself creates hazards.
Cumulative ionizing dose and radiation-sensitive organs, and it is still not recommended in pregnancy or infants
Magnetic resonance emits no ionizing radiation, so there is no dose to accumulate.

set2.io: g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: Into which spaces can contrast be injected, and what is each study called?
opts: Joints for a venogram, the central nervous system intravenously, and the bladder for a cystogram
A venogram images veins, and intrathecal is the route named for the nervous system.
Muscle for a myogram, the pleural space directly, and the ureter for an antegrade pyelogram
None of these three routes is described in the deck.
Bowel for an arthrogram, the epidural space, and the renal pelvis for a cystogram
The names are attached to the wrong spaces throughout.
Joints for an arthrogram, the central nervous system intrathecally, and the bladder for a retrograde pyelogram
Correct — three routes named besides the intravascular and enteral ones.

set2.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: How are radiographic projections named?
opts: In the position of the detector, from the cassette's near edge to its furthest corner
The detector's own geometry does not supply the name of the projection.
In the direction the beam travels, from what it strikes first to the most distal portion
Correct — so posterior-anterior means the beam enters the back and exits the front.
In the direction the patient faces, from the side nearest the film to the side furthest away
The naming follows the beam rather than which way the patient is turned.
In the order the structures appear, from the most superficial down to the deepest tissue
Projections are not named for the order in which structures are encountered on the image.

set2.io: a — Identify the fundamental properties of medical imaging
set2.q: Which four questions frame the choice of an imaging modality?
opts: Which modality the radiologist prefers, which is available today, which the insurer covers, and which is quickest
Those are practical constraints rather than the diagnostic framing.
Which modality gives the highest resolution, the largest field of view, the thinnest slices, and the fastest overall scan time for the patient
Technical parameters are not the framing questions given.
Which modality best rules the diagnosis in or out, is there a lower-radiation alternative, what is the risk against benefit for this patient, and is contrast needed
Correct — those are the four the lecture opens with.
Which modality is cheapest, which is fastest, which is closest, and which the patient prefers
Cost and availability matter but are not the framing questions given.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: On a bone scan, why are the kidneys visible?
opts: Uptake in the kidneys occurs only when renal function is impaired and clearance is slowed
Normal kidneys take up and clear the tracer; impairment is not required.
Uptake in the kidneys is normal, and the same is true of tracer on positron emission scans
Correct — the deck labels renal uptake normal on both studies.
Uptake in the kidneys indicates the tracer dose given was higher than the study required
Renal visibility is expected and says nothing about the dose administered.
Uptake in the kidneys suggests metastatic disease has reached the retroperitoneal organs
Normal renal uptake is not a finding of metastasis on either study.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What equipment does fluoroscopy require?
opts: A gamma camera mounted on a rotating gantry that circles the patient, with a fixed table and a detector housing that does not move
That describes single photon emission computed tomography.
A superconducting magnet requiring dedicated site construction beforehand and high ongoing cost
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.
A handheld transducer connected to a portable processing unit, needing neither a tilting table nor a shielded examination room
That describes ultrasound.
An x-ray unit fitted for controlled motion of the source, the imaging sensor and the patient, with a tilting table
Correct — the tube moves freely back and forth to image the patient.

set2.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Beyond the heart, what else is better seen on the posterior-anterior chest view?
opts: Maximum visualisation of the mediastinum, better visualisation of the hila, and well visualised anterior ribs
The deck names the lung fields, apices and posterior ribs rather than these.
Maximum visualisation of the diaphragm, better visualisation of free air, and well visualised gastric bubble
Free air beneath the diaphragm is what an upright abdominal series is for.
Maximum visualisation of the pleura, better visualisation of layering fluid, and well visualised costophrenic angles
Layering fluid with gravity is the decubitus view's stated purpose.
Maximum visualisation of the lung, better visualisation of the apices, and well visualised posterior ribs
Correct — all three are listed alongside the cardiac and dose advantages.

set2.io: g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: Which agent is used for fluoroscopic swallow studies, and how is the study performed?
opts: Oral technetium, with sequential gamma camera images taken as the patient swallows
Technetium is a nuclear medicine tracer rather than a swallow-study agent.
Oral barium, with sequential x-rays taken as the patient swallows it
Correct — real-time imaging is what makes fluoroscopy suit a swallow study.
Oral gadolinium, with sequential magnetic resonance images taken as the patient swallows
Gadolinium is intravenous and belongs to magnetic resonance, not fluoroscopy.
Intravenous iohexol, with sequential computed tomography images taken during swallowing
An intravascular agent does not opacify the swallowed bolus.

set2.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: A patient has free air under the diaphragm. Which history would make perforation NOT the explanation?
opts: Recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy without biopsy
That is not the exception Professor Reynolds named.
A barium swallow performed the previous week
Barium in the lumen is not free air, and this is not the named exception.
Chronic constipation with a heavy stool burden
Stool burden does not produce free intraperitoneal air.
Recent laparoscopic surgery, with the gas not yet absorbed
Correct — insufflation of the abdomen puts gas there deliberately. With belly pain, fever, nausea and vomiting and no recent surgery, it is perforation.

set2.io: g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: Which agent is named for intravenous contrast in computed tomography, and what is it?
opts: Omnipaque (iohexol), a radioactive form of iodine given into the vein
Correct — the same agent is used, at higher concentration, for angiography.
Visipaque (iodixanol), a barium salt suspension given into the vein
Iodixanol is iodinated and iso-osmolal; barium is enteral and never intravenous.
Gadolinium, a paramagnetic metal chelate given into the vein
Gadolinium is the magnetic resonance agent, not the computed tomography one.
Gastrografin, a water-soluble iodinated agent given into the vein
Gastrografin is an oral agent used when perforation is suspected.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: Which two of the five basic densities cannot be distinguished from one another on a conventional radiograph?
opts: Fat and air, which both appear black on the image
Fat is grey and somewhat darker than soft tissue, while air is blackest.
Calcium and metal, which both absorb all of the beam
Metal usually absorbs all x-rays while calcium absorbs most; they are distinguishable.
Fat and calcium, which occupy adjacent points on the scale
They sit at opposite ends of the middle range and are distinguishable.
Fluid and soft tissue, which have the same density
Correct — that limitation is one reason computed tomography expands the grey scale.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: On the Hounsfield scale, where water is zero, which tissue sits at roughly minus forty to minus one hundred and twenty?
opts: Air, which is why it reads darker than every other tissue on the scan
Air is minus one thousand, the bottom of the scale.
Fat, which is why it reads darker than soft tissue but lighter than air
Correct — fat is negative, but nowhere near as negative as air.
Soft tissue, which is why it reads darker than fat but lighter than water
Soft tissue is positive, roughly plus twenty to plus one hundred.
Bone, which is why it reads brighter than soft tissue but darker than metal
Bone is roughly plus four hundred to plus six hundred.

set2.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: How is a posterior-anterior chest film oriented when you look at it?
opts: As if you were looking at the patient's feet, with their left side on your right
That is the cross-sectional convention for tomography and magnetic resonance.
As if you were looking down from above, with their right side nearest the top
No such overhead convention is described for chest radiography.
As if the patient were standing in front of you, with their right side on your left
Correct — the same convention as facing a patient in the room.
As if the patient were standing behind you, with their right side on your right
The convention places the patient's right on your left, not your right.

set2.io: c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: Which programmable magnetic resonance technique is named as useful in stroke?
opts: Diffusion-weighted imaging, which evaluates the diffusion of water within tissue
Correct — the scanner can also be programmed to evaluate blood velocity.
Fat-suppressed imaging, which removes the signal from adipose tissue in the field
Fat suppression is not the technique the deck names for stroke.
Post-processing windowing, which re-displays the raw data over a narrower range
Post-processing and windowing are computed tomography techniques.
Gadolinium-enhanced imaging, which highlights vascular structures after injection
Contrast enhancement is used for tumours and masses rather than for stroke here.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What is a computed tomography image composed of, and what is each unit assigned?
opts: A matrix of thousands of tiny squares called pixels, each assigned a computed tomography number from −1000 to +1000 in Hounsfield units
Correct — water is assigned a Hounsfield number of zero by convention.
A matrix of thousands of tiny cubes called voxels, each assigned a greyscale signal intensity on a fixed scale running from zero to two hundred and fifty five
That is not how the lecture describes the image.
A series of two-dimensional projections, each one assigned its own radiodensity value as measured in millisieverts
Millisieverts measure radiation dose rather than image density.
A hydrogen map, each point assigned a relaxation time in milliseconds reflecting the local chemical environment of that tissue
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: On a T2-weighted image, how does tissue with high water content appear?
opts: Bright, and the examples given are fat, oedema, infection, blood and cerebrospinal fluid
Correct — remember T2 as the sequence where water is white.
Dark, and the examples given are fat, oedema, infection, blood and cerebrospinal fluid
That is the T1-weighted image; the same list simply inverts between the two.
Bright, and the examples given are cortical bone, tendon, ligament and calcified plaque
Those are low in water and in signal, and calcium emits no signal at all.
Dark, and the examples given are cortical bone, tendon, ligament and calcified plaque
This is true of those tissues but does not answer what high water content does.

set2.io: g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: What did Professor Reynolds say about the carcinogenicity of contrast media, and what does it justify?
opts: None of them is carcinogenic, which is why contrast is used freely
She stated the opposite.
Only the nuclear medicine tracers are carcinogenic, because they are radioactive
She described the contrast media generally as technically radioactive.
It is all carcinogenic
Correct — which is exactly why the diagnostic approach asks whether the study can be done without contrast. She tied the risk straight back to the four framing questions.
Only the iodinated agents are carcinogenic, which is why gadolinium is preferred
She said the risk applies to contrast media generally.

set2.io: f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: How is radiation dose defined and expressed?
opts: Ionizing energy delivered per exposure, in millisieverts only, where one millisievert is one milliwatt
A millisievert is not a unit of power and dose is not defined per exposure.
Ionizing energy absorbed per unit of mass, in grays or milligrays, where one gray is one joule per kilogram
Correct — and equivalent dose is then expressed in sieverts or millisieverts.
Ionizing energy emitted per unit of time, in grays or milligrays, where one gray is one joule per second
Dose is absorbed energy per mass, not emitted energy per time.
Ionizing energy absorbed per unit of volume, in sieverts only, where one sievert is one joule per litre
The unit of absorbed dose is the gray, and it is defined per kilogram.

set2.io: e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Which three standard planes are used in cross-sectional imaging, and how does each divide the body?
opts: Axial into upper and lower, coronal into anterior and posterior, sagittal into right and left
Correct — axial is also called transverse and is the commonest of the three.
Axial into anterior and posterior, coronal into right and left, sagittal into upper and lower
Each plane here is matched to the wrong division of the body.
Axial into right and left, coronal into upper and lower, sagittal into anterior and posterior
This rotates all three assignments and is wrong on each one.
Axial into upper and lower, coronal into right and left, sagittal into anterior and posterior
Coronal and sagittal are swapped; coronal separates front from back.

set2.io: f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: In which units is radiation measured?
opts: Tesla and gauss
Those measure magnetic field strength in magnetic resonance imaging.
Hertz and decibels
Those describe sound waves in ultrasound.
Millisieverts and milligrays
Correct — x-ray radiation is low compared with other radiographic modalities.
Hounsfield units and pixels
Hounsfield units measure computed tomography attenuation rather than radiation dose.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: Which term names an angiographic study of the veins rather than the arteries?
opts: Arthrogram, performed as either a computed tomography arthrogram or a magnetic one
An arthrogram is contrast injected into a joint, not a vascular study at all.
Venogram, performed as either a magnetic resonance venogram or a computed tomography venogram
Correct — the same modalities, aimed at the venous side.
Doppler study, performed as either a colour Doppler examination or a duplex examination
Colour Doppler shows flow in either vessel type; it is not the venous-specific term.
Coronary angiogram, performed as either a diagnostic catheterisation or an intervention
The coronary angiogram is the x-ray-based arterial study of the heart.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What is the stated trade-off of an open magnetic resonance scanner?
opts: Decreased quality of imaging, which is the price paid for the open configuration
Correct — it is available, but the deck flags the loss of quality.
Increased scan duration, which is the price paid for the open configuration
Time is listed as a general disadvantage, not as the open scanner's trade-off.
Increased radiation dose, which is the price paid for the open configuration
No magnetic resonance scanner emits ionizing radiation, open or closed.
Decreased soft tissue contrast only, with spatial resolution otherwise preserved
The deck says quality generally, without limiting it to soft tissue contrast.

set2.io: d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: On the deck's labelled pelvic radiograph, how are bone, gas and the prosthesis described?
opts: Bone is radiolucent, gas is radiopaque, and the metal prosthesis is very lucent
Each of the three labels is inverted here.
Bone is very opaque, gas is radiopaque, and the metal prosthesis is radiolucent
Metal is the most opaque of the three, not the most lucent.
Bone is radiopaque, gas is very opaque, and the metal prosthesis is radiolucent
Gas absorbs least of anything on the film, so it is lucent.
Bone is radiopaque, gas is radiolucent, and the metal prosthesis is very opaque
Correct — one image showing three of the five densities at once.

set2.io: i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set2.q: What does the deck advise when a radiology report comes back vague?
opts: Refer the patient to the relevant specialist
Onward referral is not the response the deck names to a vague report.
Contact the radiologist to discuss the patient
Correct — the relationship is described as interprofessional and team-based.
Repeat the study using a different modality
Repeating the study is not the first response the deck advises.
Order the next test in the diagnostic sequence
Moving on without clarifying the report is not what is advised.

set2.io: h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: What must be assessed before a magnetic resonance study with contrast, and why?
opts: Thyroid function, because gadolinium chelates iodine and can precipitate a thyroid storm
Gadolinium contains no iodine and this mechanism does not apply.
Nothing beforehand, because gadolinium is inert and is excreted unchanged in the bile
The deck requires assessing renal function regardless.
Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, because renal function matters primarily for clearance
Correct — gadolinium can damage kidneys, though less than iodinated contrast.
Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, because gadolinium is more nephrotoxic than iodine
The deck says the opposite: it is not as harmful as computed tomography contrast.

set2.io: b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: How are magnetic resonance images generated?
opts: A pulse of sound leaves the transducer; the echo returning from tissue is timed and plotted
That is ultrasonography, and it needs no magnetic field of any kind.
A varying magnetic field aligns hydrogen atoms; releasing it produces radio waves the computer maps
Correct — the deck calls the resulting images essentially hydrogen maps.
A varying magnetic field aligns iron atoms; releasing it produces heat the computer measures
Hydrogen is the nucleus imaged, and the signal read out is radiofrequency, not thermal.
A rotating x-ray beam passes through tissue; detectors measure how much of it is absorbed
That is computed tomography, which is why it uses ionizing radiation and this does not.
